- **OpenCode.** Don't assume Claude's nested loading or Codex's chain. Extra
  guidance files go through its explicit `instructions` configuration when a
  deployment needs them, never by loading every nested instruction globally;
  if shape scoping is required and can't be guaranteed, that is an error.
  Unrecognized frontmatter never enforces policy. `model` values are
  provider-qualified. Argument placeholders written in a command prompt are
  kept. `allowed-tools` is never an enforced command setting. Agents use
  `permission`, not the deprecated `tools`, mapped only when the meaning is
  equivalent: allow/ask/deny is not a tool list, and ambiguous conversions are
  rejected.

Other Belay diagnostics include `invalid-artifact-name`,
`missing-command-prefix`, `description-too-long`, `output-outside-project`,
`unowned-output`, `duplicated-content` and `unrepresentable-reference`.

### 11.6 Guarantees

- Identical source, configuration, directory state and toolchain produce
  identical bytes. Instructions combined into one file have a stable order.
- Frontmatter values are quoted and escaped for the target format.
- A missing reference target is reported instead of emitting a broken link.
- Unsupported metadata is reported instead of being claimed as enforced.
- Generated files are tracked in `.piton/manifest.json`, so cleanup never
  deletes files users wrote. Its `targets` records, for each target, the
  documentation date the generated files were validated against.
- Failures name the source anchor and property. Output stays inside its
  configured boundaries.

### 11.7 Open decisions

`spec/scope/belay/Decisions.pi` lists what is not decided. Tooling should say
it is unspecified rather than guess:

- Placement of instructions outside `shapeRoot`.
- The types of `tools`, `allowed-tools` and `model`, and their mapping per
  adapter.
- Naming: skill filename normalization, command name normalization before the
  `x-` prefix, acronym splitting and collision handling.
- Whether workflows stay compositions of the four constructs. Do not add a
  `workflow` keyword just because examples describe agent processes.
- How platform-specific adapter options are written.

Do not present any of these as settled. If your work depends on one, raise it
with the user.

## 12. Package management

Packages are git repositories, managed as **vendored dependencies**. Installed
packages are stored inside the project and committed to version control, and
the tooling adds, updates, removes and inspects them. Nothing is fetched at
compile time.

- **Offering packages.** A repository declares packages with `piton-package`
  anchors (`PitonPackage` from `@piton/packaging`: `name`, `root`,
  `dependencies`). A package anchor can live anywhere in the specbase but must
  be listed under `packages:` in `piton.config.pi`. A package's `root` is
  relative to `piton.config.pi`, like the project's own root. **`packages:` is what the
  repository offers to other projects; a project never installs its own
  packages.** One repository can offer several packages, each with its own
  root and dependencies.
- **Names.** `name` is what the package installs under. It exists because it
  can be kebab-case (`my-package`), which an anchor name can't. Left out, the
  anchor's own name is used. **Package names are flat: no `/`.** Names like
  `@piton/belay` are only for the packages bundled with the compiler.
- **Dependencies.** `dependencies:` lists git URLs, each with an optional
  `commit:`, `tag:` or `branch:` on an indented line beneath it (a dictionary
  item right after the URL). **Only one pin per URL**; more is
  `multiple-pins`. Without a pin, the latest commit on the default branch is
  used. **Pins are strings**: `@piton/config` types them as strings, so
  `tag: 1.0` stays `"1.0"`. Other pin diagnostics are `dangling-pin` and
  `unknown-pin`.
- **Picking packages.** A repository can offer several packages. You get all
  of them unless you list the ones you want with `packages:` under the URL:
  `packages: [ui-kit]`.
- **Project and package dependencies are separate.** The project's apply only
  to the project, and each package declares its own.
- **No nested dependencies.** When two packages need the same package at
  different versions, **the one with the newest commit wins** and a warning is
  shown.
- **Installation.** Each package goes into `tethers/<name>`, next to
  `piton.config.pi`, with the files from its `root`. A repository offering
  `ui-kit` and `my-package` gives `tethers/ui-kit` and `tethers/my-package`.
  Tethering removes every trace of git. A repository that offers no packages
  is installed whole, under the name its URL implies.
- **Importing.** An installed package is a location placeholder:
  `from my-package import X`, `use my-package`, `use my-package/MyAnchor`.
  Normal path resolution applies below it. A missing package is a compiler
  error.
- **Lock file.** `.piton/tether.lock`, next to `piton.config.pi`, keeps each
  tethered package's URL, commit and a hash of its files. `tether` and
  `update` write it, and it is committed with the project.
- **Conflicts.** Before tether, update or any other operation on an installed
  package, the tooling compares its files with the lock file and goes ahead
  only if nothing changed. If the files were edited, it says so and asks the
  user to untether (or `piton update --force` to discard the edits).

The commands:

- `piton tether` on its own installs everything in `dependencies`. Given a
  source URL, it adds it to `dependencies` in `piton.config.pi` and installs
  it. `--as <name>` installs under another name.
- `piton update [packages...] [--force] [--diff]` reinstalls from
  `dependencies`, all packages when none are named. `--force` replaces a
  package even if it was edited, discarding the edits with a warning;
  `--diff` prints a coloured unified diff of every file each update changed.
- `piton untether <package>` moves the package from `tethers/` to
  `<root>/untethered/` and rewrites the imports that named it, making it the
  project's own source. `--as <name>` renames it; `--no-rewrite` only moves
  it.
- `piton remove <package>` deletes an installed package and removes it from
  `dependencies`. It refuses if the files were edited or if anything still
  imports the package.

## 13. CLI reference

Every command prints what it produced first, then a one-line outcome (✓ or
✗), and its problems last: diagnostics, errors and warnings with their help
and notes, then the error and warning count. On a terminal the output is
coloured and paths are marked `+`/`-`; piped or with `NO_COLOR`, it is plain
text and stdout carries the bare results.

| Command | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `piton check [paths...]` | Validates syntax, imports, references, types, inheritance, composition, exports and circular dependencies, reporting errors and warnings. Writes nothing. Exits 0 when there are no errors and 1 otherwise. Paths are optional files, directories or globs; the default is the project (or every `.pi` file under the working directory when there's no `piton.config.pi`). |
| `piton build [config] [--dry-run]` | Builds the project configured by `piton.config.pi` (or the given config). Writes renderer output to `<output>/<path under root>.<ext>` (defaults: `./dist`, JSON), so `spec/components/Button.pi` becomes `dist/components/Button.json`: the entry file plus every file holding something the entry's exports reference. A registered framework's output replaces it unless the config sets `output` or `renderer`, which asks for both. Records every file in `.piton/manifest.json`. The whole plan is validated before anything is written. `--dry-run` reports without writing. |
| `piton compile <path> [--renderer json\|yaml\|markdown] [--write] [--dependencies]` | Compiles one file to stdout (JSON by default): one key per export. `--write` writes `<file>.<ext>` next to each input and is required for globs. `--dependencies` wraps the result as `{"value": "<compiled output as a string>", "dependencies": [absolute source paths]}` so build tools know what to watch; bundled package files are left out. |
| `piton format [path] [--check]` | Applies canonical formatting (4-space indents, constraint spacing, sorted and wrapped imports, no `.pi` in import paths, a space after `//`). `--check` reports without writing. `piton format -` reads source from stdin and writes the formatted text to stdout. It **only splits overflowing lines and never rejoins a paragraph**, so rewrap edited prose by hand, and don't reflow `key: value` blocks as prose. |
| `piton reach [targets...] [--no-unreachable] [--no-paths]` | Starting from files, globs or anchor names (the entry by default), follows outgoing imports, references, inheritance and composition, direct and transitive. Reports what is reachable with its depth and the path taken, and what is unreachable. The flags hide the last two. Use it to find dead spec. Grouped by source, with a summary. No diagnostics; always exits 0. |
| `piton slice <target> [--adapter <target>]` | Prints the part of the spec one thing depends on, as one Markdown document for an agent's prompt. The target is `file.pi#Anchor`, `file.pi#Anchor.property`, `file.pi#variable`, or a bare name looked up across the project (an error when more than one file declares it). Follows, transitively: what an anchor extends, every base that also declares a property, anchors named by type constraints, what a value read (`${Other.x}`, variables), and what it references or embeds. Imports alone bring nothing in. A whole anchor needs all its properties and bases; slicing a property leaves out the anchor's other properties; a reference to a property needs only that property. It also includes the **chain** from the project's entry down to the target (`Specification.Tooling`, `Tooling.cli`, `Cli.commands`): the shortest path the build takes, each link only that one property and not followed further. An export of the entry, a variable, and a file the build doesn't reach have no chain. Order: the target, then its dependencies nearest first (source order breaks ties), then the chain outermost first, so the same source prints the same bytes. Each declaration appears once, headed by its name as written (`SaveButton.color`), with its file, what it extends, its type and what it reads. References and embeds are written as names; cycles are followed until they come back around. Every path it prints is relative to the directory it runs in, and it finds the project by looking upward for `piton.config.pi`. `--adapter claude-code` (any Belay target the project builds) cites the compiled output instead: each location and every reference links to where `piton build` writes it (an embedded anchor to the section that embeds it), and no `.pi` file is ever cited; an abstract base or an anchor that is only read has no document of its own and is described without one. With `--adapter` the target itself must be something the build writes out. Markdown links the author wrote pass through unchanged. Exits 1 on errors. |
| `piton init [directory] [--template <group/name>] [--adapter <id>...] [--list]` | Starts a new project from a template compiled into the compiler (no network needed). Templates come in groups: `piton/minimal` (plain Piton to JSON), `piton/library` (a package others can tether), `belay/application` (a shape instruction placed in `src/`, a skill, an agent and a command) and `belay/minimal` (the Belay config and one skill). Without a directory it first asks for the project's name and creates that directory (an empty answer, or no terminal, uses the working one). Then it asks for a group and a template (`--template belay` asks only for the template), and for a Belay template, which adapters to build for: a checklist of Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode with the template's default (Claude Code) checked, or `--adapter`, repeated or comma-separated. The chosen adapters replace the config's import and `adapters` list, and a template's `.adapters/<id>/` files (like OpenCode's `opencode.json`) are written only for the adapters chosen. Templates are the `group/name` directories in the compiler repo's `create-templates/`, each with a one-line `.template` description that is not written out; adding one is adding a directory, and every template must check cleanly, be formatted, and build. `--list` describes the groups and templates and does nothing else. With no terminal, a full template name is required. It never overwrites a file: if any it would write exists, it names each and writes none, and cancelling a question writes nothing. Prints each written path on stdout, then a summary and the next commands on stderr. Exits 1 on errors. |
| `piton loc [paths...]` | Counts total, code, comment and blank lines per file, with a summary. Defaults to the project. No diagnostics; always exits 0. |
| `piton lsp` | Runs the language server over stdio (section 14). |
| `piton agent [claude] [--print-fluency] [args...]` | Launches the agent with a short project primer plus this fluency prompt (the project's `FLUENCY_PROMPT.md`, or the copy built into the compiler), passed to `claude` as `--append-system-prompt`. Extra arguments go to the agent. `--print-fluency` prints the prompt and does nothing else. |
| `piton tether [source] [--as name]` | See section 12. |
| `piton update [packages...] [--force] [--diff]` | See section 12. |
| `piton untether <package> [--as name] [--no-rewrite]` | See section 12. |
| `piton remove <package>` | See section 12. |

Each CLI command in the spec is a `cli-command` anchor
(`spec/scope/tooling/cli/index.pi`) with `commandName`, `positionalArguments`
and `namedArguments`.

## 14. Language server, editors, and JavaScript

`piton lsp` provides, from the spec's feature list:

- Diagnostics (not for missing optional properties), completion, hover (type,
  source, documentation, inheritance chain, export status and compiled
  interpretation), go-to-definition, find-references, and rename across the
  whole specbase.
- Auto-import, import organization, and code actions: import a missing
  symbol, create an unresolved anchor, add an export, qualify an ambiguous
  reference, resolve a simple inheritance conflict.
- Document and workspace symbols, semantic highlighting, inlay hints
  (resolved types, inherited origins, composition sources), formatting,
  folding and selection ranges.
- Inheritance, composition (`+`, `++`), override and conflict resolution;
  reference resolution; validation and type information for expressions in
  `{}`, `${}`, `#{}` and `@{}`; export validation; module resolution; cycle
  detection (circular imports are fine and not reported).
- Related-symbol navigation, a hierarchy view, resolved-value and provenance
  inspection, compiled-output preview, source-to-output mapping, unused and
  redundant definition detection, and documentation integration.
- Incremental analysis and workspace indexing.
- Diagnostics cover Belay semantics as well as Piton. Import organization
  flags unused, duplicate, invalid and overly broad imports. Cycle detection
  also catches an anchor that ends up extending itself, and shows the cycle.

There is no signature help.

Completion rules: never suggest things that don't exist; offer nothing on an
empty value (`property: `), because prose probably follows; offer nothing
after a `.` inside a string.

Editing rules every editor must follow, through the LSP or the editor
extension:

- Enter after a colon that opens a dictionary or anchor property starts a new
  line indented one level deeper.
- Enter on a blank line inside a dictionary or anchor starts a new line one
  level shallower.
- Format-on-save is optional. It adds the space after `//` and touches nothing
  else that is commented.

Supported editors and their highlighters (spec): VS Code (TextMate plus LSP);
Emacs, Helix and Zed (tree-sitter plus LSP); Neovim and Vim (vim syntax);
JetBrains (`jetbrains`); Sublime (sublime-syntax); Kate (KSyntaxHighlighting).
Every editor gets full LSP support. The integrations live under `editors/`.

**Consuming Piton from JavaScript.** `packages/vite-plugin-piton` imports
`.pi` files as modules, with HMR, dependency tracking (through
`piton compile --dependencies`) and virtual modules. Each export in the Piton
file is a named export, and the default export is the whole file, the same as
`piton compile` gives:

```ts
import { SaveButton } from '../spec/app.pi';
import spec from '../spec/app.pi';

const button = SaveButton;
const cancel = spec.CancelButton;
```

It has a configurable default renderer (`renderer: 'json' | 'yaml' |
'markdown'`), and the renderers can also be imported as functions
(`vite-plugin-piton/renderers`) and used inline. `packages/astro-piton` is an
Astro integration that wraps the Vite plugin.

## 15. Working on a specbase

1. **Orient.** Open `piton.config.pi` to find `root`, `entry`, `output`, the
   frameworks, the adapters, `codeRoot` and `shapeRoot`. Read the entry file,
   usually `spec/index.pi`, because its exports are the compilation roots.
   Follow the `index.pi` files down through the modules. In this repository,
   `spec/index.pi` exports `Specification` (FoundingThesis, Language, Tooling,
   Belay, PackageManagement) plus the skills and command in `spec/agent/`.
2. **Read compiled reference for overview, and source for truth.**
   `<referenceRoot>/**/*.md` is easy to browse, and its links are lazy, so
   follow them only when relevant.
3. **Edit the `.pi` source**, following the conventions around it:
   - one exported anchor per file, named after the file;
   - `index.pi` files that re-export with `from ./X export *`;
   - abstract anchors exported with a keyword, and shared abstracts in a
     `lib/` folder;
   - lowerCamelCase property names;
   - SCREAMING_CASE for exported constant lists;
   - prose in string blocks, and structure in keys and lists;
   - `@{X}` to link related documents;
   - examples inside fences wrapped in a `\\\` escape block.
4. **Keep imports honest.** Use `use` for keywords and `from ... import` for
   names; a file often needs both. A new file only compiles if the entry
   reaches it, so export it through an index or reference it.
5. **Validate.**
   - Run `piton check`.
   - `piton check` does **not** compile the examples inside escape blocks
     (they are literal text). When you edit spec examples, extract each ` ```piton ` block,
     run `piton compile` on it, and compare with any ` ```json ` block that
     follows. Remember that compile output has only exported names.
   - Run `piton build`, then look at the diff of the generated files.
   - Run `piton reach` to confirm new anchors are reached.
   - Run `piton format --check`.
6. **Never hand-edit generated files.** That includes `CLAUDE.md` and
   `AGENTS.md` under `codeRoot`, everything under `.claude/`, `.codex/`,
   `.agents/`, `.opencode/` and the build output directory that is listed in
   `.piton/manifest.json`, and the files in `.piton/` themselves.
7. **Keep implementation and spec in agreement.** The implementation is judged
   against the spec. When they disagree, report it instead of quietly bending
   the spec to fit. Trust `piton compile` for how things behave today, and
   flag the gap.

## 16. Where the compiler differs from the spec

Checked with `piton compile` and `piton build`:

- The CLI has a few things the spec doesn't name: `build --dry-run`,
  `tether --as`, agent argument passthrough, the `reach` flags, and
  `format` with no path or `-`.

- **Paragraph breaks.** The spec says a blank line in a string block starts a
  new paragraph. The compiler joins the paragraphs with a single `\n`, which
  Markdown output renders as one paragraph with a soft line break.

Known limitations, where the spec is silent and the compiler's choice may
surprise you:

- A `/`-rooted import inside an installed package resolves against the
  consuming project's root, not the package's. Use relative imports inside a
  package.
- A required property from an abstract is not satisfied by a value inherited
  from a concrete base (`needs Thing extends Base`, where `Base` supplies it):
  the keyword's anchor comes last, and its value-less declaration wins. Give
  the value on the anchor itself.
- `piton check` with no paths checks what the entry reaches, so a file that
  nothing imports is not checked. Name it: `piton check path/to/file.pi`.
- **Prose directly in an anchor body is silently dropped.** `anchor A:` with
  only a line of text under it (no key) compiles to an empty anchor, with no
  diagnostic. Always put prose under a key, such as `description:`.
- Mixed-type equality is simply unequal: `{1 == "1"}` is `false`, not an
  error. The spec says `==` works on every type but doesn't spell this out.
- Which constructs each adapter requires a `description` for (section 11.2)
  is hardcoded in `crates/piton-belay/src/adapter.rs`, not declared in the
  adapter `.pi` files.

# Harness Integration

## Pitch

Uses the one-off version of a coding harness for the selected ProjectDirectory: `claude -p`, `codex exec`, or `opencode run`, whichever the user chose. Each run carries on a conversation, so the harness keeps its context between requests.

## Description

Should always run in auto mode.
The project's system prompt, its system template filled in, as the [ModeSystemPrompts](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts) says, is appended to the harness's own system prompt, for example with `--append-system-prompt`, the same for every prompt of a conversation whatever its mode. The compiled systemPrompt of a prompt's hidden anchor, its mode's instructions, heads the prompt's own message instead.
The prompt is given to the harness on its standard input, and what the harness does is streamed back as it happens. A task's run takes its prompt as a stream of messages rather than a single one, so it can be fed more while it works, as its feeding says.
Its directory, which a system prompt's HARNESS_DIRECTORY stands for, is that of the harness in use: .claude, .codex, or .opencode.
Every run, whatever its mode, runs the harness natively on the host, in the project directory, under the sandbox of its mode's profile, as the [Sandbox](../sandbox/index.md#sandbox) says, which lets it read and change only what its mode may: a Code run never the spec's source, a Spec run never the code. The harness is run, prompted, and read just as this says, whatever its profile.

## Harnesses

The harness in use is the project's: Claude Code, Codex, or OpenCode, a setting of each project, saved with its data, as the [ProjectData](../project-data/index.md#project-data) says, picked when the project is created or imported and changed in the [SettingsWindow](../settings-window/index.md#settings-window). Each open project runs with its own, so two projects open side by side can use different harnesses. A project with no harness saved, as one made before this or opened from elsewhere, uses the first harness its piton.config.pi builds for, by its adapters in order, Claude Code for ClaudeCodeAdapter, Codex for CodexAdapter, OpenCode for OpenCodeAdapter, or Claude Code where it builds for none, and saves that as its own the first time it is opened. Runs the application makes outside any project, as with no project open, use Claude Code. Every run the application starts goes to it, the tasks, the questions, the palette's file search, the one-off runs, and the notes, commit messages, and prompt titles it writes, and everything else works the same whichever it is. A run already going when another is picked finishes with the harness it started with, and a conversation is only carried on by the harness it began with; the next request with another harness starts a new one.
Each harness is run its own way, streaming what it does as a line of JSON per event, which is read into the same reply, tool calls, usage, and result, whichever harness wrote it:

- Claude Code is `claude -p`, in auto mode, the system prompt given with `--append-system-prompt`, a conversation carried on with `--resume`, and a copy of one with `--fork-session`, its output `--output-format stream-json` with `--verbose` and `--include-partial-messages`, so its reply streams in as it is written, token by token, with the usage of each message as it goes, for every run, tasks of every mode and questions alike.
- Codex is `codex exec`, with `--full-auto` and `--json`, the prompt read from its standard input, a conversation carried on with `resume`.
- OpenCode is `opencode run`, with `--format json`, a conversation carried on with `--session`.

Codex and OpenCode take no system prompt of their own, so it is given ahead of the prompt, marked off from it. Neither can carry on a copy of a conversation, so a question asked while another is running starts a new conversation with them instead. The notes, commit messages, and prompt titles are written with a small model where the harness can be told one, Claude Code's haiku, and with the harness's default model otherwise.
No run the application starts is given the connectors of the user's claude.ai account, such as Gmail, Google Calendar, or Google Drive, whatever its profile, whatever the account has connected or left unauthorized: Claude Code is run with them turned off, with `ENABLE_CLAUDEAI_MCP_SERVERS` set to `false` in its environment. So the harness is never told that a connector needs authorizing or is still connecting, never searches for or calls one, and never passes such a notice on in what it replies, and nothing of the kind is ever shown in a task's output, a question's answer, or anywhere else. MCP servers the project itself configures are left as they are, and run under the run's sandbox as anything it starts does.
When the harness picked isn't installed, a run fails saying that it can't be run, as any run that can't be started does, and one whose sandbox can't be applied fails saying so, as the [Sandbox](../sandbox/index.md#sandbox) says.

## Protected Locations

What a run may read and change is enforced by its sandbox, as the [Sandbox](../sandbox/index.md#sandbox) says, never by watching files or putting anything back: the application never reverts, restores, or deletes any file a run changed. A Code run can't read or change the spec's source at all, and reads the compiled reference instead, as the [ModeSystemPrompts](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts) says; a Spec run can't read or change the code, but where the project lets it read the code. The harness is still told, where it takes rules for its tools, as Claude Code does with `--disallowedTools`, what its profile keeps it off, so it doesn't waste a turn trying, but that is only a courtesy: the sandbox is what enforces it. A Freeform run may change the project, but for its data and its `.git`, and is told nothing.

## Feeding

A task's run is given its prompt as a stream of messages: Claude Code with `--input-format stream-json`, each message written as a line of JSON on the harness's standard input, which stays open for as long as the run lasts. The run's first message is the task's compiled prompt, as ever, and each message sent to the task after it, from the [ChatInput](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input), is written as another.
A message reaches the harness when it finishes what it is doing rather than interrupting it, so a run that is mid-tool-call takes it once that call is over. The harness echoes each message back as it takes it in, with `--replay-user-messages`. A message taken in between turns is answered with a result of its own, and one taken while a turn is under way is answered within that turn, sharing its result.
A run can also start work in the background that goes on after its turn ends: Claude Code's subagents, shell commands run in the background, such as a long build, and any other kind of background task it adds later. Every such task holds the run open, whatever its kind. The run keeps each background task that has started and not yet ended, by its id: one starts when the harness says a task has started, and ends when the harness notifies that task's end, whatever it ended as. A notification doesn't say what kind of task it is, so it is matched by id against those seen starting. The harness wakes the run when a background task ends, so it can act on what came of it.
Each background task is known by its kind, from what started it: a subagent, started by an Agent or Task tool call, or a command, a shell command run in the background. Its start is when the harness said it had started, so how long it has been running can be told. A single background task can be stopped while the run goes on, without ending the run or any other task: the harness is asked, on the run's input, to stop that task by its id, Claude Code with its stream-json control request for stopping a task. The task then ends when the harness notifies its end, as ever, as stopped, and the harness carries on with what came of it. Stopping one is never done by stopping the harness's process, and a run whose input is already closed, or whose harness can't be fed, can't stop one on its own.
A result no longer ends the task on its own. The run's last result is the first to come once every message sent has been taken in and no background task is still going. A result that comes before then, while a message sent hasn't been taken in or a background task is still going, is only an answer: the task keeps running, its input stays open, and more can still be sent to it. At the last result the run's input is closed, but the task is only shown as finished once the harness's process has exited as well, and it then finishes in the state of that last result; until the process exits, the task keeps running. A process that exits without a last result finishes the task as a run with no result does, failed. A run that is stopped closes its input and ends straight away, whatever is still going in the background, since its whole process group is ended with it.
A background command that never ends on its own, as a dev server started with `npm run dev`, `vite`, or `node server.js`, or a watcher, never keeps a task running once its work is done. Once a result has come, every message sent has been taken in, and no subagent is still going, a background command still running holds the run open only while it is busy: one that has printed nothing for 60 seconds since that result, as a server does once it has started and waits for requests, is taken as idle. Once every background task left is an idle command, the run asks the harness to stop each of them, as a single background task is stopped above, and once their ends are notified, the result that came is the run's last, and the task finishes in its state, done where it was. A command that keeps printing, as a long build or test run does, keeps the run open until it ends or goes quiet. While the run waits on background commands and nothing else, the task's status still reads "Running", and its tooltip says it is waiting on background commands, naming how many, which the subagents panel lists with their Stop buttons.
A harness's process that hasn't exited 10 seconds after the run's last result, with its input closed, as when a server it started still holds its output open, is ended with its whole process group, and the task finishes in the state of that last result, never left running. Whatever the run started is ended with it: no server a task started is left running once the task is shown as finished, so its port is free again.
Codex's `codex exec` and OpenCode's `opencode run` read a single prompt and can't be fed more while they work, so a task running with either takes its prompt as ever and can't be sent more.
Questions, the palette's file search, the one-off runs, and the notes, commit messages, and prompt titles each take a single prompt, as ever.

## Images

Images attached to a prompt, as the [ChatInput](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input) says, are given to the harness as it takes them: to Claude Code as image content blocks, base64-encoded with their media type, in the same stream-json user message as the prompt's text, after it; to Codex with an `--image` argument per image; and to OpenCode with a `--file` argument per image. A message fed to a running Claude Code task carries its images the same way, and a Claude Code run that isn't fed more but has images is given its prompt as a stream-json message too, so the images can go with it. Codex's options end with `--` before the prompt when it is given images. Questions take images as tasks do.

## Context

The harness keeps its context between requests instead of starting fresh each time. Each lane of the [PromptSending](../prompt-mode/sending/index.md#prompt-sending) carries on a conversation of its own, so nothing a task of one lane read reaches a task of the other: the spec lane's, carried on by Spec tasks and a Chain prompt's spec steps, and the code lane's, carried on by Code tasks, a Chain prompt's code step, and Freeform tasks. Each task sent carries on its own lane's, and since a lane runs one task at a time, two tasks never carry on the same conversation at once. A Chain prompt's steps hand on to each other as text, the prompt and what the step before replied, as the [ModeSystemPrompts](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts) says, so the handoff crosses lanes whatever each lane's conversation holds. When the project is opened, each lane carries on the latest conversation among its own tasks in the history, a Chain task by the lane of the step it was.
Every run keeps its conversation's sessions where the harness keeps them on the host, as `~/.claude`, which its sandbox grants it, and each is also copied into the project after every run, as below, so it carries on across runs, restarts of the application, and moves of the project.
Questions from the Ask tab share a separate conversation of their own, and when the project is opened they carry on the latest conversation among the questions saved with it. A question asked while another is running carries on a copy of that conversation, so questions running at the same time never write over each other. A conversation is only carried on in the project it began in, each open project keeping its own tasks' and questions' conversations while it is in the background. A conversation from before its sessions were copied into the project, or whose session was kept in a container before the sandbox replaced them, is still tried, and when the harness has no such session and the project holds no copy of it, the request is sent again at once as a new conversation, as below.
A request whose conversation can't be carried on, because the harness says it has no such session, as Claude Code's "No conversation found", or because it was begun elsewhere, is never failed for it. Its session is first put back from the project's copy, as above, and the request carried on with it; only where there is no copy, or it still can't be carried on, is it never retried on the same conversation: it is sent again at once as a new conversation, the same prompt, with no context, and the conversation it couldn't carry on is not tried again by any later request, the project's history included. A question sent again so is recorded and shown as starting a new conversation, as the [AskConversation](../prompt-mode/ask-conversation/index.md#ask-conversation) marks one. Each run applies its own prompt's systemPrompt, even when it carries on a conversation begun in a different mode. The palette's file search always starts fresh.
A conversation the application carries on never expires on its own. Every Claude Code run the application starts, whatever its profile, is run with its transcript cleanup turned off, as its `cleanupPeriodDays` setting given so that no session is ever old enough to be deleted, passed with the run rather than written to the user's own settings, so Claude Code never deletes a session for its age.
When a run is over, however it ended, the application copies the harness's session for its conversation, its transcript and whatever the harness needs to resume it, into the project's data, beside the run's history record, as the [ProjectData](../project-data/index.md#project-data) says, replacing the copy an earlier run of the same conversation left. # Harness Integration

## Pitch

Uses the one-off version of a coding harness for the selected ProjectDirectory: `claude -p`, `codex exec`, or `opencode run`, whichever the user chose. Each run carries on a conversation, so the harness keeps its context between requests.

## Description

Should always run in auto mode.
The project's system prompt, its system template filled in, as the [ModeSystemPrompts](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts) says, is appended to the harness's own system prompt, for example with `--append-system-prompt`, the same for every prompt of a conversation whatever its mode. The compiled systemPrompt of a prompt's hidden anchor, its mode's instructions, heads the prompt's own message instead.
The prompt is given to the harness on its standard input, and what the harness does is streamed back as it happens. A task's run takes its prompt as a stream of messages rather than a single one, so it can be fed more while it works, as its feeding says.
Its directory, which a system prompt's HARNESS_DIRECTORY stands for, is that of the harness in use: .claude, .codex, or .opencode.
Every run, whatever its mode, runs the harness natively on the host, in the project directory, under the sandbox of its mode's profile, as the [Sandbox](../sandbox/index.md#sandbox) says, which lets it read and change only what its mode may: a Code run never the spec's source, a Spec run never the code. The harness is run, prompted, and read just as this says, whatever its profile.

## Harnesses

The harness in use is the project's: Claude Code, Codex, or OpenCode, a setting of each project, saved with its data, as the [ProjectData](../project-data/index.md#project-data) says, picked when the project is created or imported and changed in the [SettingsWindow](../settings-window/index.md#settings-window). Each open project runs with its own, so two projects open side by side can use different harnesses. A project with no harness saved, as one made before this or opened from elsewhere, uses the first harness its piton.config.pi builds for, by its adapters in order, Claude Code for ClaudeCodeAdapter, Codex for CodexAdapter, OpenCode for OpenCodeAdapter, or Claude Code where it builds for none, and saves that as its own the first time it is opened. Runs the application makes outside any project, as with no project open, use Claude Code. Every run the application starts goes to it, the tasks, the questions, the palette's file search, the one-off runs, and the notes, commit messages, and prompt titles it writes, and everything else works the same whichever it is. A run already going when another is picked finishes with the harness it started with, and a conversation is only carried on by the harness it began with; the next request with another harness starts a new one.
Each harness is run its own way, streaming what it does as a line of JSON per event, which is read into the same reply, tool calls, usage, and result, whichever harness wrote it:

- Claude Code is `claude -p`, in auto mode, the system prompt given with `--append-system-prompt`, a conversation carried on with `--resume`, and a copy of one with `--fork-session`, its output `--output-format stream-json` with `--verbose` and `--include-partial-messages`, so its reply streams in as it is written, token by token, with the usage of each message as it goes, for every run, tasks of every mode and questions alike.
- Codex is `codex exec`, with `--full-auto` and `--json`, the prompt read from its standard input, a conversation carried on with `resume`.
- OpenCode is `opencode run`, with `--format json`, a conversation carried on with `--session`.

Codex and OpenCode take no system prompt of their own, so it is given ahead of the prompt, marked off from it. Neither can carry on a copy of a conversation, so a question asked while another is running starts a new conversation with them instead. The notes, commit messages, and prompt titles are written with a small model where the harness can be told one, Claude Code's haiku, and with the harness's default model otherwise.
No run the application starts is given the connectors of the user's claude.ai account, such as Gmail, Google Calendar, or Google Drive, whatever its profile, whatever the account has connected or left unauthorized: Claude Code is run with them turned off, with `ENABLE_CLAUDEAI_MCP_SERVERS` set to `false` in its environment. So the harness is never told that a connector needs authorizing or is still connecting, never searches for or calls one, and never passes such a notice on in what it replies, and nothing of the kind is ever shown in a task's output, a question's answer, or anywhere else. MCP servers the project itself configures are left as they are, and run under the run's sandbox as anything it starts does.
When the harness picked isn't installed, a run fails saying that it can't be run, as any run that can't be started does, and one whose sandbox can't be applied fails saying so, as the [Sandbox](../sandbox/index.md#sandbox) says.

## Protected Locations

What a run may read and change is enforced by its sandbox, as the [Sandbox](../sandbox/index.md#sandbox) says, never by watching files or putting anything back: the application never reverts, restores, or deletes any file a run changed. A Code run can't read or change the spec's source at all, and reads the compiled reference instead, as the [ModeSystemPrompts](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts) says; a Spec run can't read or change the code, but where the project lets it read the code. The harness is still told, where it takes rules for its tools, as Claude Code does with `--disallowedTools`, what its profile keeps it off, so it doesn't waste a turn trying, but that is only a courtesy: the sandbox is what enforces it. A Freeform run may change the project, but for its data and its `.git`, and is told nothing.

## Feeding

A task's run is given its prompt as a stream of messages: Claude Code with `--input-format stream-json`, each message written as a line of JSON on the harness's standard input, which stays open for as long as the run lasts. The run's first message is the task's compiled prompt, as ever, and each message sent to the task after it, from the [ChatInput](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input), is written as another.
A message reaches the harness when it finishes what it is doing rather than interrupting it, so a run that is mid-tool-call takes it once that call is over. The harness echoes each message back as it takes it in, with `--replay-user-messages`. A message taken in between turns is answered with a result of its own, and one taken while a turn is under way is answered within that turn, sharing its result.
A run can also start work in the background that goes on after its turn ends: Claude Code's subagents, shell commands run in the background, such as a long build, and any other kind of background task it adds later. Every such task holds the run open, whatever its kind. The run keeps each background task that has started and not yet ended, by its id: one starts when the harness says a task has started, and ends when the harness notifies that task's end, whatever it ended as. A notification doesn't say what kind of task it is, so it is matched by id against those seen starting. The harness wakes the run when a background task ends, so it can act on what came of it.
Each background task is known by its kind, from what started it: a subagent, started by an Agent or Task tool call, or a command, a shell command run in the background. Its start is when the harness said it had started, so how long it has been running can be told. A single background task can be stopped while the run goes on, without ending the run or any other task: the harness is asked, on the run's input, to stop that task by its id, Claude Code with its stream-json control request for stopping a task. The task then ends when the harness notifies its end, as ever, as stopped, and the harness carries on with what came of it. Stopping one is never done by stopping the harness's process, and a run whose input is already closed, or whose harness can't be fed, can't stop one on its own.
A result no longer ends the task on its own. The run's last result is the first to come once every message sent has been taken in and no background task is still going. A result that comes before then, while a message sent hasn't been taken in or a background task is still going, is only an answer: the task keeps running, its input stays open, and more can still be sent to it. At the last result the run's input is closed, but the task is only shown as finished once the harness's process has exited as well, and it then finishes in the state of that last result; until the process exits, the task keeps running. A process that exits without a last result finishes the task as a run with no result does, failed. A run that is stopped closes its input and ends straight away, whatever is still going in the background, since its whole process group is ended with it.
A background command that never ends on its own, as a dev server started with `npm run dev`, `vite`, or `node server.js`, or a watcher, never keeps a task running once its work is done. Once a result has come, every message sent has been taken in, and no subagent is still going, a background command still running holds the run open only while it is busy: one that has printed nothing for 60 seconds since that result, as a server does once it has started and waits for requests, is taken as idle. Once every background task left is an idle command, the run asks the harness to stop each of them, as a single background task is stopped above, and once their ends are notified, the result that came is the run's last, and the task finishes in its state, done where it was. A command that keeps printing, as a long build or test run does, keeps the run open until it ends or goes quiet. While the run waits on background commands and nothing else, the task's status still reads "Running", and its tooltip says it is waiting on background commands, naming how many, which the subagents panel lists with their Stop buttons.
A harness's process that hasn't exited 10 seconds after the run's last result, with its input closed, as when a server it started still holds its output open, is ended with its whole process group, and the task finishes in the state of that last result, never left running. Whatever the run started is ended with it: no server a task started is left running once the task is shown as finished, so its port is free again.
Codex's `codex exec` and OpenCode's `opencode run` read a single prompt and can't be fed more while they work, so a task running with either takes its prompt as ever and can't be sent more.
Questions, the palette's file search, the one-off runs, and the notes, commit messages, and prompt titles each take a single prompt, as ever.

## Images

Images attached to a prompt, as the [ChatInput](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input) says, are given to the harness as it takes them: to Claude Code as image content blocks, base64-encoded with their media type, in the same stream-json user message as the prompt's text, after it; to Codex with an `--image` argument per image; and to OpenCode with a `--file` argument per image. A message fed to a running Claude Code task carries its images the same way, and a Claude Code run that isn't fed more but has images is given its prompt as a stream-json message too, so the images can go with it. Codex's options end with `--` before the prompt when it is given images. Questions take images as tasks do.

## Context

The harness keeps its context between requests instead of starting fresh each time. Each lane of the [PromptSending](../prompt-mode/sending/index.md#prompt-sending) carries on a conversation of its own, so nothing a task of one lane read reaches a task of the other: the spec lane's, carried on by Spec tasks and a Chain prompt's spec steps, and the code lane's, carried on by Code tasks, a Chain prompt's code step, and Freeform tasks. Each task sent carries on its own lane's, and since a lane runs one task at a time, two tasks never carry on the same conversation at once. A Chain prompt's steps hand on to each other as text, the prompt and what the step before replied, as the [ModeSystemPrompts](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts) says, so the handoff crosses lanes whatever each lane's conversation holds. When the project is opened, each lane carries on the latest conversation among its own tasks in the history, a Chain task by the lane of the step it was.
Every run keeps its conversation's sessions where the harness keeps them on the host, as `~/.claude`, which its sandbox grants it, and each is also copied into the project after every run, as below, so it carries on across runs, restarts of the application, and moves of the project.
Questions from the Ask tab share a separate conversation of their own, and when the project is opened they carry on the latest conversation among the questions saved with it. A question asked while another is running carries on a copy of that conversation, so questions running at the same time never write over each other. A conversation is only carried on in the project it began in, each open project keeping its own tasks' and questions' conversations while it is in the background. A conversation from before its sessions were copied into the project, or whose session was kept in a container before the sandbox replaced them, is still tried, and when the harness has no such session and the project holds no copy of it, the request is sent again at once as a new conversation, as below.
A request whose conversation can't be carried on, because the harness says it has no such session, as Claude Code's "No conversation found", or because it was begun elsewhere, is never failed for it. Its session is first put back from the project's copy, as above, and the request carried on with it; only where there is no copy, or it still can't be carried on, is it never retried on the same conversation: it is sent again at once as a new conversation, the same prompt, with no context, and the conversation it couldn't carry on is not tried again by any later request, the project's history included. A question sent again so is recorded and shown as starting a new conversation, as the [AskConversation](../prompt-mode/ask-conversation/index.md#ask-conversation) marks one. Each run applies its own prompt's systemPrompt, even when it carries on a conversation begun in a different mode. The palette's file search always starts fresh.
A conversation the application carries on never expires on its own. Every Claude Code run the application starts, whatever its profile, is run with its transcript cleanup turned off, as its `cleanupPeriodDays` setting given so that no session is ever old enough to be deleted, passed with the run rather than written to the user's own settings, so Claude Code never deletes a session for its age.
When a run is over, however it ended, the application copies the harness's session for its conversation, its transcript and whatever the harness needs to resume it, into the project's data, beside the run's history record, as the [ProjectData](../project-data/index.md#project-data) says, replacing the copy an earlier run of the same conversation left. Before carrying on a conversation whose session the harness no longer has, as when it was cleaned up, the machine changed, or the session was kept on the host and the harness's own folder was cleared, it puts the latest copy back where the harness looks for it, under the same session id, so the conversation carries on with its context rather than starting a new one. Only where no copy of it exists, or it can't be put back, is the request sent again as a new conversation, as below, and a conversation the user left for a new one is never restored.

A conversation can be left for a new one, from the chat input's New conversation button, as the [ChatInput](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input) says, which leaves the conversation of the lane it is used for: the next request in it starts a new conversation with no context, and the one left is not carried on again, not by a run of it still going, nor by the project's history. Leaving it is kept with the project, as the [ProjectData](../project-data/index.md#project-data) says, so a project opened after a lane's or the questions' conversation was left starts a new one there too, rather than carrying on the latest conversation in its history, until a run after the reset begins one of its own. How much context a conversation holds is known from what the harness reports with each reply: everything the model was given, cached or not, and what it wrote, as of its latest reply; replies of subagents don't count.

A task shows it in its output and a question at the end of its answer. It never reads only "the harness reported an error", or any other message that leaves the cause unnamed; a generic line is only ever a heading above what the harness said. A run that couldn't be started says why it couldn't, and one whose sandbox couldn't be applied says so, as the [Sandbox](../sandbox/index.md#sandbox) says.

3:## Description
4-
5-A task's status is a coloured label that spells it out: "Building" in blue, "Compiling" in cyan, "Running" in yellow, "Done" in green, "Failed" in red, "Cancelled" in orange, "Paused" in the theme's warning colour for a task paused to be resumed, as the PromptSending says, "Stopped" in grey for a chain that stopped short of a step it was to run, and "Not recorded" in grey for a task from the history with no record of its run. The labels are readable in both light and dark mode.
6-
7-## Alignment
8-
9-The spinner, the status label, the elapsed time, and the output rate read as one line, wherever they show together. Each is centred on the line's middle, the spinner and the label's box alike, so none sits higher or lower than the others, and the label's text and the times share one baseline. They are one text size, small: the label's text is no larger than the times beside it. The spinner is 12 pixels square, drawn the colour of the status label, never larger than the label's text is tall. The label is a pill 20 pixels tall, its text with 6 pixels to each side, its 1 pixel border and faint fill in its own colour, corners rounded 4 pixels. They are 6 pixels apart throughout, spinner to label, label to time, and time to rate, the same gap on each side, never wider on one side than the other.
10-
11-## Elapsed
12-
13-Beside its status label, a task shows how long it has been under way, from when it was sent, building and compiling included, in small muted tabular figures: minutes and seconds, "0:42" or "12:05", with hours ahead of them once it reaches an hour, "1:02:33". While the task is building, compiling, or running, it counts up every second, so a task that seems stuck can be told from one that has only just started. Once the task is over, however it ended, it stops and stays at how long the task took. It shows wherever the status label does, the latest task's header and the heading of each previous task, including a task running in the other lane. A task from the history whose record holds no start and end, as one recorded before they were kept, shows how long it took as well as can be told, from the second its history file is named by to when its record was written, with "≈" before it, as "≈ 4:12", its tooltip saying it is approximate; one where neither can be told shows none.
14-In the Tasks tab, every task's row shows how long it took, as the latest task's header does, though not beside its status: done, failed, or cancelled alike, and a task still running there counting up. A chain's parent row shows the time its steps took together, from when its first step was sent to when its last ended, and each step's heading beneath it its own. The times line up, right-aligned in their own column of the heading, just before its buttons, so the list reads as a column of durations that can be compared at a glance, and a long one stands out.
15-
42:## Chained Tasks
43-
44-A prompt sent in Chain runs as steps, each saved in the history as a task of its own: first the Chain task itself, which writes the spec; then the same prompt sent to Code, told what the spec step did; and, when the chain asks for a post-build spec update, the same prompt sent to Spec once more, told what the code step did. Each step knows the one it was sent from, as the [PromptSending](./sending/index.md#prompt-sending) says. Only the steps the chain sends itself belong to it; a task sent to the other mode by hand, or resent, from one of its steps is a task of its own.
45-Each step runs in the lane of the work it does, as the [PromptSending](./sending/index.md#prompt-sending) says: the Chain task and its spec follow-up in the spec lane, the code step in the code lane. A step is sent once the step before it finishes, never before, and takes its place in its lane's queue by when its chain was sent, not when the step itself was: behind every prompt waiting there that was sent before its chain, earlier chains' steps included, and ahead of every prompt sent after it. So a chain's code step never jumps ahead of a Code prompt, or another chain's code step, sent before the chain was, and a Code prompt sent while the chain's spec step ran waits for the chain's code step rather than coming between the chain's steps. Two steps whose chains were sent in the same order run in that order, whichever spec step finished first. Where nothing sent before its chain is waiting, it runs as soon as its lane is free, and straight away if it already is. Its place holds however it came to be queued, so a restart, with the queue read back from the project, keeps it there. The lane it leaves is free for its own queue meanwhile, so a Spec task sent while a chain's code step runs runs beside it. A step waiting for its lane shows in the queue like any prompt, and can be cancelled there, ending the chain. A step whose chain step before it failed or was cancelled is never sent.
46-Each step also runs under the sandbox of the work it does, as the [Sandbox](../sandbox/index.md#sandbox) says: the spec steps under the Spec profile, which can't reach the code, and the code step under the Code profile, which can't reach the spec's source. Each carries on its own lane's conversation, as the [HarnessIntegration](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration) says, so a step is told what the step before it did only through its prompt: the Chain prompt as typed and that step's final output, as the [ModeSystemPrompts](./mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts) says.
47-In the Tasks tab, a chain is one row, as the [TasksTab](../../ui/components/right-sidebar/tasks/index.md#tasks-tab) says, holding its steps, so they read as parts of a single chain: a joined chain icon, the first line of the prompt, and at its right how many steps it has, "2 steps" or "3 steps". Its status is the chain's as a whole, worked out only from its steps as they actually are, never from what the chain might still do: Running, with its spinner and its time counting, while one of its steps is building, compiling, or running now, in this project's runs, and while one of its steps waits in a lane's queue after an earlier step of it has run, as its code step queued behind another task once its spec step is done: the chain is under way, though that step is queued. It reads Running too between its steps, while a step of it has ended Done and the application is still to send the next, in this session: building the spec on the host after its spec step, compiling the next step, or waiting for that step's name, so it never reads Done for even a moment while a step it will run is still to come. A multi-step task is Done only once every step it was to run is Done; until then, a step of it Done is only that step's status, never the chain's. It reads Queued, in the theme's muted colour, only while it hasn't started, its first step still waiting in the queue and none of its steps run yet. Otherwise it is over: Failed or Cancelled if a step was; Done only where every step it was to run is Done; Not recorded where a step has no record of its run; and, where it stopped short of a step it was to run, with no step failed or cancelled, as when the application closed between its steps, Stopped, in the theme's muted colour, never Done. A chain whose later step was never sent, as one from before chains sent them or one whose application closed between its steps, is over, reading Stopped, its parent saying muted after its step count that its code step was never sent, and never reads Running or Done for it. What the application is still to send is known only in the session that sent the chain: after a restart, a chain whose next step wasn't sent or queued has stopped.
48-Each step's state is read from where it truly is: a step is running only while the application has its run under way, which no step from the history ever does after a restart, since every run ends when the application quits; queued only while its prompt is in the queue; and otherwise from its own history record, a step with no record of its run reading Not recorded, never Running. Steps are joined to their chain only by which step each was sent from, as below, so a task never takes the state of a chain it doesn't belong to, and a chain never counts a task that isn't one of its steps.
37:## Sprint
38-
39-Stories move among Draft, the Backlog, and Next sprint by dragging, as the [DragReorderBehaviour](../../ui/behaviours/drag-reorder/index.md#drag-reorder-behaviour) says, a card dragged by its grip from one of them into a gap in another as within any one, the gap opened in the column the pointer is over, as motion says; an empty one takes a drop at its top. Dragged near the board's left or right edge, the board scrolls sideways, and near a column's top or bottom, that column scrolls, as dragging says. # Mode System Prompts

## Pitch

The system prompt each mode sends, which tells the harness what kind of work a prompt is, and which each project can make its own.

## Description

What a prompt tells the harness besides itself comes in two parts. The system template is the conversation's system prompt: the same for every prompt of a conversation, whatever its mode, so the harness's prompt cache holds when the mode changes. Each lane's tasks, and the questions, carry on a conversation of their own, as the [HarnessIntegration](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration) says, and each fills the system template in for what its runs can see, so it stays the same within each. Each of the [PromptModes](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes) but Freeform has instructions of its own, which change from one prompt to the next, and so go in the prompt's own message, in a block marked <task-instructions> at its head. A prompt's hidden anchor has a systemPrompt property, alongside its userPrompt, holding its mode's instructions.

## Templates

The system template, each mode's instructions, and the injected prompts are Piton prose, like the prompt they are sent with, so they can reference the spec, with these placeholders, each written after a dollar sign and inside braces like a Piton interpolation:

- CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION, the code location and the spec location, as the [ProjectLocations](../../project-locations/index.md#project-locations) says
- HARNESS_DIRECTORY, the directory of the harness in use
- SPEC_READING, the spec-reading prompt, injected where it is written
- PITON_FLUENCY_FILE, the path of the fluency file, from the project directory, as the pitonFluency below says
- SUSPENSE_FLUENCY_FILE, the path of the Suspense fluency file, from the project directory, as the suspenseFluency below says
- UNDERSTANDING_FILE, the path of the task's understanding file

SPEC_READING is filled in first, so the placeholders it holds are filled in too; then the others, before the prompt is compiled, but UNDERSTANDING_FILE, which is filled in as the prompt is sent, once the task's history record is named, so a prompt sent from the queue is given its own. A question from the Ask tab has no understanding file, and UNDERSTANDING_FILE is filled in with nothing. Each can be moved or removed, like any other text of a template.
Every path a placeholder is filled in with points where the run that is sent it finds that file, and that its sandbox lets it reach, as the [Sandbox](../../sandbox/index.md#sandbox) says. So each is written relative to the project directory, the directory every run works in: CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION as `./` and the location's path, as `./spec`, HARNESS_DIRECTORY as the harness's directory, as `.claude`, and PITON_FLUENCY_FILE, SUSPENSE_FLUENCY_FILE, and UNDERSTANDING_FILE as their paths, as `.suspense/fluency.md`. None is ever filled in with an absolute path.
A run fills CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION in only with what it can see, as its sandbox's profile allows, as the [Sandbox](../../sandbox/index.md#sandbox) says. A run of the spec lane, a Spec task or a Chain prompt's spec step, can't see the code location, and fills CODE_LOCATION in with nothing, its instructions and system template alike, unless the project lets its Spec runs read the code, as the [Sandbox](../../sandbox/index.md#sandbox) says, when it fills CODE_LOCATION in as a question does, and is told, on a paragraph of its own, that the code there is read only, for reading what the spec describes, never for changing, and, where they may read the whole project too, that everything in the project directory is there to read, read only. A question can see the code location and the spec location, both read only, and fills both in. A run of the code lane, a Code task, a Chain prompt's code step, or a Freeform task, runs on the host and fills both in, as ever.
A paragraph that held nothing but a placeholder filled in with nothing goes with it. A paragraph holding CODE_LOCATION or SPEC_LOCATION filled in with nothing goes too, whatever else it says, so no prompt names, or tells the harness to keep off, a location its run can't see. A paragraph holding PITON_FLUENCY_FILE or SUSPENSE_FLUENCY_FILE, filled in with nothing, goes too, whatever else it says, so a sentence pointing at a fluency file there is none of is never sent. A template left with nothing but blank space once filled in gives nothing at all.
HARNESS_DIRECTORY is the directory the harness that runs the prompt, as the [HarnessIntegration](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration) says, reads its agentic Markdown and reference files from, written without a leading ./: .claude for Claude Code, .opencode for OpenCode, and .codex for Codex, the directories the [NewProject](../../new-project/index.md#new-project) names for them.

## Reading The Spec

In every mode, the harness learns what the spec says from its compiled reference, the Markdown the spec build writes under HARNESS_DIRECTORY's reference folder, where inheritance, expressions, and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what `piton slice` prints for it with the adapter of the harness in use. It never reads the Piton source under the spec location to learn what the spec says. To a run that can see the spec location, the system template and the spec-reading prompt say so, and name the spec location only as where edits to the spec go. A question sees the spec location too, read only, so it can run `piton slice` there, and is told the same: that the spec is read from the compiled reference or from what `piton slice` prints, never from the Piton source. A question makes no edits, so the Ask instructions name the spec location for what it is, the spec's Piton source, that `piton slice` reads, which a question never changes, and nothing told to a question says or suggests that it may edit the spec. A run that can't see the spec location is told only that the spec is read from the compiled reference, with nothing about the spec source.

## Writing The Spec

Only Spec, and a Chain prompt's first step, which writes the spec, work on the Piton source. Their instructions say to open a .pi file only to change it, since a harness may need a file read before it can edit it, and, once the edits are made, to run `piton build` and check the result in the refreshed reference rather than by reading the source again.

## Piton Fluency

The Piton fluency, what `piton agent --print-fluency` prints, run in the project directory, is how Piton is written. It is never part of the system prompt: only work that writes Piton is pointed at it.
It is written to the fluency file, `.suspense/fluency.md` in the project's data, as the [ProjectData](../../project-data/index.md#project-data) says, each time the application runs a spec build in the project, as the [SpecBuild](../../spec-build/index.md#spec-build) says, so it keeps in step with the project's piton and its FLUENCY_PROMPT.md. A Spec or Chain prompt sent before the file has ever been written has it written before the prompt is compiled. What it prints is written as text, never read as Piton, but for the project directory's absolute path on the host wherever it appears in it, which is written as `.` instead, a path within it as relative to it, as `./spec`, so the file holds no path of the machine it was written on.
PITON_FLUENCY_FILE stands for the file's path. The Spec instructions and the Chain instructions, for a Chain prompt's first step, say, on a paragraph of their own, to read that file once in the conversation before creating or editing any .pi file. A Code task sent to Spec is pointed at it through the Spec instructions, as any Spec prompt is. The Code and Ask instructions, and the spec-to-code prompt given to a Chain prompt's code step, never mention it.
Where `piton` isn't installed, or printing the fluency fails, no file is written, and PITON_FLUENCY_FILE is filled in with nothing, so the paragraph pointing at it is left out.

Every mode but Freeform is pointed at it, so a question asked to write a Chain prompt, or a task asked about the queue, knows what that is, in a project that says nothing of Suspense itself. Like the Piton fluency, it is never part of the system prompt, so the prompt cache holds whatever the mode.
It is the same for every project, and is the application's own, not a project's to edit: its source is a Markdown file in this application's own repository, `suspense-fluency.md` in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory beside the defaults, baked into the application when it is built, as they are, so a build always ships with whatever it says, and a build can't be made without it. It is written to the Suspense fluency file, `.suspense/suspense-fluency.md` in the project's data, as the [ProjectData](../../project-data/index.md#project-data) says, before any Code, Chain, Spec, or Ask prompt is compiled, whenever the file isn't there or doesn't hold what the application ships, so it keeps in step with the application rather than the project. The spec-reading prompt explains how to read the spec before executing anything, as the readingTheSpec above says: from the compiled reference, reference links in the prompt being the spec for what they name, each read before anything it covers is changed. ## Defaults

Don't re-read anything you've already read.
The Spec and Chain defaults have, after what the mode is for, on a paragraph of its own:
Before creating or editing any .pi file, read ${PITON_FLUENCY_FILE} once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Piton is written.
and then, on another:
Open a .pi file only to change it. Once you have changed the spec, run `piton check` and fix every error it reports, then run `piton build` and check the result in the refreshed reference under ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference, not by reading the source again. The Code, Chain, and Spec defaults then end with, on a paragraph of its own:
Once you have read what the change depends on, and before your first change, write the constraints this task must meet to ${UNDERSTANDING_FILE}, once. End with a reply of a few sentences saying what changed, or for a question, the answer, not a recap of the work or of what you read.
So a task spends as few turns as it can before doing the work: it reads the pages the prompt links to and what the change depends on through them, never a survey of the spec, never a page given to it as a slice, and writes its understanding once, between its reading and its first change.
The Code, Chain, Spec, and Ask defaults each have, after what the mode is for, on a paragraph of its own:
When the work is about Suspense, its modes, its prompts, or its questions, or you are to write a prompt or a question for the user, first read ${SUSPENSE_FLUENCY_FILE} once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Suspense works.

Since a question can see the spec location, that paragraph is always sent with it.
The Ask default says nothing of how an answer hands back prompts and questions: that is the card format below, which every question is given whatever its project's Ask instructions say.
The Spec and Chain defaults never name the code location, and the Code default names the spec location only on a paragraph of its own, which goes where the run can't see it.

Each of the [PromptModes](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes) but Freeform has instructions of its own, which change from one prompt to the next, and so go in the prompt's own message, in a block marked <task-instructions> at its head. ## Templates

The system template, each mode's instructions, and the injected prompts are Piton prose, like the prompt they are sent with, so they can reference the spec, with these placeholders, each written after a dollar sign and inside braces like a Piton interpolation:

- HARNESS_DIRECTORY, the directory of the harness in use
- SPEC_READING, the spec-reading prompt, injected where it is written
- PITON_FLUENCY_FILE, the path of the fluency file, from the project directory, as the pitonFluency below says
- SUSPENSE_FLUENCY_FILE, the path of the Suspense fluency file, from the project directory, as the suspenseFluency below says
- UNDERSTANDING_FILE, the path of the task's understanding file

SPEC_READING is filled in first, so the placeholders it holds are filled in too; then the others, before the prompt is compiled, but UNDERSTANDING_FILE, which is filled in as the prompt is sent, once the task's history record is named, so a prompt sent from the queue is given its own. A question from the Ask tab has no understanding file, and UNDERSTANDING_FILE is filled in with nothing. Each can be moved or removed, like any other text of a template.
