It is not a project's to edit or leave out: the application adds it to each question's <task-instructions> block, after the project's Ask instructions, on a paragraph of its own, whatever those say, including a project's Ask instructions saved before it was added, which are kept as they are. Its text is baked into the application from this application's own repository, in `ask-cards.md` in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory beside the defaults, and a build can't be made without it. It is never given to a task, and Freeform sends nothing. It says:
Whenever the user asks you for a prompt, or your answer suggests one for them to send, give each prompt as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-prompt` and the mode it is for, one of `code`, `chain`, `spec`, `ask`, or `freeform`, such as ```` ```suspense-prompt chain ````, holding only the prompt's text, ready to send, never as plain text, a quote, or any other code block, since only this form lets the user send it from your answer. Pick the mode that fits the work, `chain` when it changes both the spec and the code; the user can send it to Code, Chain, or Spec all the same. When you need the user to answer something before you can go on, write the question as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-question`, the question on its first lines and then, if there are answers to pick from, one per line, each starting with `- `. Use these blocks only for prompts and questions meant for the user, never for code or examples.

## Resuming

The resume prompt is the message given to a paused task when it is resumed, as the [PromptSending](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending) says, sent on its own as the next message of the task's conversation, never compiled as a prompt. Like the injected prompts, each project has its own, saved with its data in resume.md beside the templates, and edited in the [SettingsWindow](../../settings-window/index.md#settings-window); with no file yet the project uses its default, which says:
Your previous run on this task was interrupted before it finished. Any step you were in the middle of, such as an edit, a command, or a build, may not have completed, and files may have changed since. Before carrying on, check the state of what you were working on: re-read the files you were changing and re-run any check you need. Then carry on from where you left off; don't start the task over or redo work that is already done.

## Saving

Each project has its own system template, instructions, and injected prompts, saved with its data, as the [ProjectData](../../project-data/index.md#project-data) says, a Markdown file each, system.md for the system template, code.md, combined.md for Chain, spec.md, and ask.md for the modes, and edited in the [SettingsWindow](../../settings-window/index.md#settings-window). One with no file yet gives its default.

## Understanding File

Each Code, Chain, or Spec task has an understanding file: the short list of constraints the harness has taken from the spec for it, which the [LeftSidebar](../../../ui/components/left-sidebar/index.md#left-sidebar)'s Run view shows as it changes. It is saved beside the task's history record, with the same name and the extension `.understanding.md`, written by the harness itself. Nothing else writes it, and nothing is there until the harness writes it. Each constraint links to the compiled reference file it comes from, never to the spec's source.

## Defaults

The defaults are the prompts saved in this application's own repository, in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory, named as a project's are. They are the source of truth for the defaults, and are baked into the application when it is built, so a build always ships with whatever those files say, and changing them changes the defaults the next build has. A build can't be made without them.
The system template's default says what the project is, where its code is and where its spec is, each on a paragraph of its own, so the one a run can't see goes, that each prompt starts with a <task-instructions> block saying what that prompt is for and what it may change, and then SPEC_READING on a paragraph of its own. It holds no fluency.
The spec-reading prompt's default says:
Read the spec from its compiled reference under ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference, where inheritance, expressions, and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what `piton slice` prints for it with this harness's adapter.

Never read the .pi source under ${SPEC_LOCATION} to learn what the spec says; that is only where edits to the spec go.

Read only what the change depends on, and start the work as soon as you have. Links to ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference/... in the prompt are the spec for what they name: read those, and then only the pages they link to that the change actually depends on. Don't survey the spec, list its folders, or search it before you start. A page the prompt already gives you as a slice is already read: never read it again. Don't re-read anything you've already read.
The Spec and Chain defaults have, after what the mode is for, on a paragraph of its own:
Before creating or editing any .pi file, read ${PITON_FLUENCY_FILE} once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Piton is written.
and then, on another:
Open a .pi file only to change it. Once you have changed the spec, run `piton check` and fix every error it reports, then run `piton build` and check the result in the refreshed reference under ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference, not by reading the source again. Never finish with a spec that `piton check` or `piton build` reports errors in.
The Code, Chain, and Spec defaults then end with, on a paragraph of its own:
Once you have read what the change depends on, and before your first change, write the constraints this task must meet to ${UNDERSTANDING_FILE}, once. Rewrite it only when a constraint in it turns out to be wrong, never after each page you read. It is a Markdown list and nothing else: one line per constraint, at most twelve, each a single short, specific statement of what must be true, written as a link to the compiled reference file it comes from, such as `- [The chain tab has no bottom border in combined mode](${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chain)`. Only list what the spec says; leave out anything you are deciding yourself. Replace a constraint when you learn it was wrong rather than adding another.
The Code, Chain, Spec, and Ask defaults end, on a paragraph of its own, by asking for a short final reply:
End with a reply of a few sentences saying what changed, or for a question, the answer, not a recap of the work or of what you read.
So a task spends as few turns as it can before doing the work: it reads the pages the prompt links to and what the change depends on through them, never a survey of the spec, never a page given to it as a slice, and writes its understanding once, between its reading and its first change.
The Code, Chain, Spec, and Ask defaults each have, after what the mode is for, on a paragraph of its own:
When the work is about Suspense, its modes, its prompts, or its questions, or you are to write a prompt or a question for the user, first read ${SUSPENSE_FLUENCY_FILE} once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Suspense works.
The Ask default says what a question is for, and that it changes nothing, and, on a paragraph of its own, that SPEC_LOCATION is the spec's Piton source, there for `piton slice`, which the question reads the spec through, read only and never edited, and never read directly to learn what the spec says. Since a question can see the spec location, that paragraph is always sent with it.
The Ask default says nothing of how an answer hands back prompts and questions: that is the card format below, which every question is given whatever its project's Ask instructions say.
The Spec and Chain defaults never name the code location, and the Code default names the spec location only on a paragraph of its own, which goes where the run can't see it.
The defaults are only where a project starts, and what resetting a prompt puts back. A project whose prompts were saved before a default changed keeps them as they are.

        carries on its own lane's, and since a lane runs one task at a time,
        two tasks never carry on the same conversation at once. A Chain
        prompt's steps hand on to each other as text, the prompt and what the
        step before replied, as the @{ModeSystemPrompts} says, so the
        handoff crosses lanes whatever each lane's conversation holds. When
        the project is opened, each lane carries on the latest conversation
        among its own tasks in the history, a Chain task by the lane of the
        step it was.

        Every run keeps its conversation's sessions where the harness keeps
        them on the host, as `~/.claude`, which its sandbox grants it, and
        each is also copied into the project after every run, as below, so
        it carries on across runs, restarts of the application, and moves of
        the project.

        Questions from the Ask tab share a separate
        conversation of their own, and when the project is opened they carry on
        the latest conversation among the questions saved with it. A question
        asked while another is running carries on a copy of that conversation,
        so questions running at the same time never write over each other. A
        conversation is only carried on in the project it began in, each open
        project keeping its own tasks' and questions' conversations while it is
        in the background. A conversation from before its sessions were
        copied into the project, or whose session was kept in a container
        before the sandbox replaced them, is still tried, and when the
        harness has no such session and the project holds no copy of it, the
        request is sent again at once as a new conversation, as below.

        A request whose conversation can't be carried on, because the
        harness says it has no such session, as Claude Code's "No
        conversation found", or because it was begun elsewhere, is never
        failed for it. Its session is first put back from the project's
        copy, as above, and the request carried on with it; only where there
        is no copy, or it still can't be carried on, is it never retried on
        the same conversation: it is sent again at once as a new
        conversation, the same prompt, with no
        context, and the conversation it couldn't carry on is not tried
        again by any later request, the project's history included. A
        question sent again so is recorded and shown as starting a new
        conversation, as the @{AskConversation} marks one. Each run applies
        its own prompt's systemPrompt, even when it carries on a conversation
        begun in a different mode. The palette's file search always starts
        fresh.

        A conversation the application carries on never expires on its own.
        Every Claude Code run the application starts, whatever its profile,
        is run with its transcript cleanup turned off, as its
        `cleanupPeriodDays` setting given so that no session is ever old
        enough to be deleted, passed with the run rather than written to the
        user's own settings, so Claude Code never deletes a session for its
        age.

        When a run is over, however it ended, the application copies the
        harness's session for its conversation, its transcript and whatever
        the harness needs to resume it, into the project's data, beside the
        run's history record, as the @{ProjectData} says, replacing the
        copy an earlier run of the same conversation left. Before carrying on
        a conversation whose session the harness no longer has, as when it
        was cleaned up, the machine changed, or the session was kept on the
        host and the harness's own folder was cleared, it puts the latest
        copy back where the harness looks for it, under the same session id,
        so the conversation carries on with its context rather than starting
        a new one. Only where no copy of it exists, or it can't be put back,
        is the request sent again as a new conversation, as below, and a
        conversation the user left for a new one is never restored.

        Codex and OpenCode sessions are kept and restored the same way,
        wherever each harness keeps them: Codex's under its sessions folder,
        and OpenCode's in its data directory, each copied after a run and put
        back before one that needs it. A session is restored into the
        harness's own folder on the host.

        A conversation can be left for a new one, from the chat input's New
        conversation button, as the @{ChatInput} says, which leaves the
        conversation of the lane it is used for: the next request in it
        starts a new conversation with no context, and the one left is not
        carried on again, not by a run of it still going, nor by the project's
        history. Leaving it is kept with the project, as the @{ProjectData}
        says, so a project opened after a lane's or the questions' conversation
        was left starts a new one there too, rather than carrying on the latest
        conversation in its history, until a run after the reset begins one of
        its own. How much context a conversation holds is
        known from what the harness reports with each reply: everything the
        model was given, cached or not, and what it wrote, as of its latest
        reply; replies of subagents don't count.

    failures:
        A run that fails always says what went wrong, in the harness's
        own words, which are the error its result carries, or the error events it
        streamed, and where it gave none, what it printed on its standard
        error, and its exit status, as written. A task shows it in its
        output and a question at the end of its answer. It never reads
        only "the harness reported an error", or any other message that
        leaves the cause unnamed; a generic line is only ever a heading
        above what the harness said. A run that couldn't be started says
        why it couldn't, and one whose sandbox couldn't be applied says so, as
        the @{Sandbox} says.

    bakedPrompts: @{BakedSystemPrompts}

        A task's run can also fail without any error from the harness, when
        its reply says it couldn't do the work: that it failed, that it
        couldn't write or change what it was to, that the sandbox or a
        missing file blocked it, or that it gave up. Such a task is Failed,
        never Done. This is never guessed from the wording of the reply: the
        run says it in its verdict, a line every task is asked to end its
        reply with, as the @{ModeSystemPrompts} says, and the application
        reads only that. The verdict is the last line of the reply of the
        run's last result that isn't blank, trimmed, read without regard to
        case: `SUSPENSE-VERDICT: done` where it did the work, and
        `SUSPENSE-VERDICT: failed` where it didn't. Where that line reads
        failed, the task finishes Failed, with the "Failed" label of the
        @{MessageListStatus}, though the harness reported success. Where it
        reads done, or the reply gives no verdict, as a Freeform task's or
        one sent with a project's own instructions that leave it out, the
        task finishes in the state of its last result, as the feeding says;
        a verdict never makes a run that failed Done.

        A task failed by its verdict says why in the run's own words, as
        every failed run does: its output shows its reply, which says what
        stopped it, beneath a heading saying the run reported that it
        couldn't do the work. The verdict line itself is never shown in a
        task's output, nor handed on as part of its final output, to a
        chain's next step or anywhere else. The task is saved as Failed in
        its history record, its reply with it, so it reads Failed after a
        restart too, and never Done.

        Being Failed, it is followed by everything that follows a failed
        task: in a chain, the next step is never sent and the chain reads
        Failed, as the @{PromptEditor}'s chained tasks say; in Planning, its
        story's card shows Failed, the story never counts as Done, Close
        sprint sends it back to the start of Next sprint rather than into
        Done, and Start automatically doesn't start the next sprint because
        of it, as the @{Planning} says.

content.content:
A run that fails always says what went wrong, in the harness's own words, which are the error its result carries, or the error events it streamed, and where it gave none, what it printed on its standard error, and its exit status, as written. A task shows it in its output and a question at the end of its answer. It never reads only "the harness reported an error", or any other message that leaves the cause unnamed; a generic line is only ever a heading above what the harness said. A run that couldn't be started says why it couldn't, and one whose sandbox couldn't be applied says so, as the [Sandbox](../sandbox/index.md#sandbox) says.
A task's run can also fail without any error from the harness, when its reply says it couldn't do the work: that it failed, that it couldn't write or change what it was to, that the sandbox or a missing file blocked it, or that it gave up. Such a task is Failed, never Done. This is never guessed from the wording of the reply: the run says it in its verdict, a line every task is asked to end its reply with, as the [ModeSystemPrompts](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts) says, and the application reads only that. The verdict is the last line of the reply of the run's last result that isn't blank, trimmed, read without regard to

### Case

`SUSPENSE-VERDICT: done` where it did the work, and

`SUSPENSE-VERDICT: failed` where it didn't. Where that line reads failed, the task finishes Failed, with the "Failed" label of the [MessageListStatus](../prompt-mode/message-list/Status.md#message-list-status), though the harness reported success. Where it reads done, or the reply gives no verdict, as a Freeform task's, the task finishes in the state of its last result, as the feeding says; a verdict never makes a run that failed Done.
A task failed by its verdict says why in the run's own words, as every failed run does: its output shows its reply, which says what stopped it, beneath a heading saying the run reported that it couldn't do the work. The verdict line itself is never shown in a task's output, nor handed on as part of its final output, to a chain's next step or anywhere else. The task is saved as Failed in its history record, its reply with it, so it reads Failed after a restart too, and never Done.
Being Failed, it is followed by everything that follows a failed

### Task

content.text:
I've written the verdict rule into the spec. `piton check` reports no problems and `piton build` succeeds; I checked the result in the rebuilt reference.

**What the spec now says**
- **The verdict line:** every Code, Chain and Spec task, chain steps included, must end its reply with exactly `SUSPENSE-VERDICT: done` or `SUSPENSE-VERDICT: failed`. When it fails, the reply says what stopped it before that line.
- **Always sent:** the application adds this request itself, like the card format, so a project's own saved instructions can't leave it out. Its text is baked in from `.suspense/system-prompts/task-verdict.md`. Questions, resume messages and Freeform tasks don't get it.
- **How it's read:** only the last non-blank line of the last result's reply counts, trimmed and ignoring case. Nothing else in the wording is looked at.
- **What follows:** if the line says `failed`, the task finishes Failed even though the harness reported success. A `done` line or no verdict keeps today's behaviour, and a verdict never turns a failed run into Done.
- **Output:** the task shows its reply under a heading saying the run reported it couldn't do the work. The verdict line is stripped from the displayed output and from what is handed to the next chain step. The task is saved as Failed in its history record, so it still reads Failed after a restart.
- **Downstream:** being Failed, everything that already follows a failed task applies to chains and Planning.

**Anchors for the code to follow**
- `HarnessIntegration.feeding` — a task finishes in the state of its last result unless the verdict says it failed.
- `HarnessIntegration.failures` — reading the verdict, the Failed state, the output heading, stripping the line, the history record, and the chain and Planning effects.
- `ModeSystemPrompts.verdict` (new) — which tasks get the request, where it goes, and its exact text, which the code needs to put in `task-verdict.md`.
- `ModeSystemPrompts.suspenseFluency` — the shipped Suspense fluency file should also say prompts never include the verdict line themselves.
